questions.prompt: What gap did AMSI (Antimalware Scan Interface) specifically close for security products?
options: It let antivirus products scan network traffic for the first time
It let a security product inspect script content immediately before execution, even for code generated dynamically and never written to disk
It only applies to files downloaded from the internet
questions.explanation: Before AMSI, security products could scan files at rest but had no reliable way to inspect script content built and executed entirely in memory. AMSI gives them a hook to inspect that content right before it runs.

questions.prompt: What is the actual purpose of PowerShell's -ExecutionPolicy Bypass flag?
options: It disables Windows Defender for the current session
It is a convenience/safety feature controlling script-signing prompts, not a security boundary -- Microsoft's own documentation says so directly
It is required to run any PowerShell script at all
questions.explanation: Execution Policy governs whether scripts need a signature or confirmation prompt to run. It's explicitly not a security boundary, which is why its presence alone is a weak signal compared to other indicators in this lesson.

questions.prompt: Why does invoking the PowerShell 2.0 engine (powershell -version 2) evade both AMSI and modern Script Block Logging in one step?
options: PowerShell 2.0 has stronger security than later versions
Both AMSI and Script Block Logging were added to PowerShell after version 2.0 existed, so the legacy engine predates them entirely
Version 2 requires administrator rights to invoke, which blocks most attackers
PowerShell 2.0 has been completely removed from all modern Windows versions
questions.explanation: AMSI and Script Block Logging were both introduced well after PowerShell 2.0. Explicitly invoking the legacy engine sidesteps both by running code in an environment that never had either capability.

questions.prompt: In an environment where Constrained Language Mode (CLM) is the documented, expected policy, what should a session running in Full Language Mode suggest to an analyst?
options: Nothing -- Full Language Mode is always the default and expected
Either a policy gap or an active attempt to escape the intended restriction, worth investigating
That the host has PowerShell 7 installed
That Script Block Logging is disabled
questions.explanation: Constrained Language Mode is an actual hardening control via WDAC/AppLocker. Full Language Mode where CLM is expected indicates either a misconfiguration or a deliberate bypass -- either way, worth investigating.
